incident_details.title: High Risk Alerts: ESA for 192.168.20.201
incident_details.description: The alert shows unusual host-originated network activity from 192.168.20.201 to multicast/NetBIOS destinations (239.255.255.250:1900 and 192.168.20.255:137). There is no evidence of malware execution, PowerShell abuse, exfiltration, or file activity, so this is best treated as suspicious behavior requiring investigation rather than an active compromise.

requested_gaps: step_3: Was any malicious process spawned on the victim's machine?
step_4: Analyze the process tree for signs of malicious activity, such as privilege escalation, lateral movement, or data exfiltration.
step_1: Identify 1. username 2. IP address 3. Login Details 4. Computer name 5. Operating System

gap_findings.step_3: No malicious process is evidenced in the supplied incident data. The alert is network-only and centers on a single UDP session from 192.168.20.201:62099 to multicast 239.255.255.250:1900 with the alert title 'Chu Wen - Lateral Move Detected.' There are no process fields populated (process_vid, filename, launch_argument, parent/child references, hash, analysis_service, hostname, user, operating_system are blank), so the data does not show any spawned executable, script, or service on the victim host. The presence of SSDP/multicast traffic can indicate discovery or noisy network behavior, but it is not proof of process execution.
gap_findings.step_4: Process tree analysis is not possible from the incident data because no process telemetry exists in the alert payload. However, the network clue indicates likely lateral-movement-oriented behavior rather than vertical escalation: the source is 192.168.20.201 and the alert references source trail admin2@192.168.20.14, both in the same 192.168.20.0/24 subnet, which is consistent with internal east-west traffic. The destination 239.255.255.250:1900 is a multicast SSDP address, so this specific event looks more like local network discovery/broadcast activity than direct exfiltration. There is no evidence of privilege escalation, process spawning, or data exfiltration in the provided data.
gap_findings.step_1: Identity and host context are mostly missing in the incident payload. The only username-like clue is 'admin2@192.168.20.14:50005' in the source trail, suggesting an administrative account or a sensor/source context tied to admin2, but the alert's user fields are blank and no authenticated username is confirmed. The victim/source IP is 192.168.20.201, source MAC is 00:0c:29:df:de:7e, destination is 239.255.255.250:1900, and the host summary repeats 192.168.20.201:62099 to 239.255.255.250:1900. Computer name and operating system are not present. Login details are not present beyond the source trail string, which may reflect the investigative source rather than an end-user logon.

actionable_queries.step_3: Collect host telemetry from the endpoint 192.168.20.201: query EDR for process creation events (Sysmon Event ID 1, Windows Security 4688, or EDR process-start telemetry) around 2025-07-15 08:14 UTC; run EDR parent/child process tree search for PID/ppid lineage on that host; if available, review PowerShell logs (Event ID 4104) and Script Block logs for the same time window.
actionable_queries.step_4: Query the endpoint's process tree and network connections: Sysmon Event ID 1 (process creation), 3 (network connection), 11 (file creation), 12/13/14 (registry), and Security 4688; on host 192.168.20.201 run 'tasklist /v', 'wmic process get ProcessId,ParentProcessId,Name,CommandLine', 'Get-Process | Select Name,Id,Path', and 'netstat -ano' to correlate processes with sockets; if lateral movement is suspected, query Windows Security 4624/4625/4672/4776 and 4768/4769 for logon and Kerberos activity.
actionable_queries.step_1: Pull endpoint identity from host inventory and authentication logs: query EDR asset inventory for 192.168.20.201 to retrieve hostname and OS; query Windows Security Event ID 4624 (logon) and 4648 (explicit credentials) for usernames; query DHCP logs or DNS records for hostname-to-IP mapping; if the source trail admin2@192.168.20.14 is relevant, inspect the source sensor or NetWitness investigation context to determine whether it is the analyst/source system rather than the victim user.

triage_deep_dive.deep_dive_summary: The supplied evidence is a network-only ESA alert with no host process telemetry, so no malicious process or process tree can be confirmed from the incident record. The strongest clue is internal east-west traffic on the same 192.168.20.0/24 network to SSDP multicast 239.255.255.250:1900, which is more consistent with discovery/lateral-movement-related activity than privilege escalation or exfiltration. Identity, hostname, and OS remain missing and require endpoint inventory/authentication log c
